Developers, Marketplaces and the Answer Engines

Analysislowob research

By lowob · 16 April 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 7-minute read · Distribution

AI distribution runs through the platforms you plug into, the assistants buyers ask, and the people who build on you. Pick one lead motion, layer the compounding channels, and spend on paid last. The evidence for each channel is now concrete: 45% of B2B buyers in Gartner's 2026 survey had used generative AI during a purchase, cloud marketplaces let buyers spend committed cloud budgets on your product, and product-led adoption carried 27% of AI application spend in Menlo Ventures' 2025 survey.

Pick a lead motion

Developer-led, sales-led, partner-led. Each needs a different company. Pick one to lead and let the others support.

MotionWhen it fitsWhat it needs
Developer-ledDevelopers choose the tool and it lives inside their codeAn API, docs that work on the first try, a free tier, fast answers in public
Sales-ledThe buyer is a department, the data is sensitive and the contract is largeThe pilot design from Part 12 and a security pack before the first call
Partner-ledThe product only makes sense inside another platformIntegration depth and a partner manager who answers the phone

Trying all three at once with one small team is how a seed-stage company spends a year reaching nobody.

The developer-led case is stronger in AI than in older software. Menlo Ventures' 2025 survey of 495 US enterprise AI decision makers found 27% of AI application spend came through product-led growth, against 7% for traditional software, with adoption often starting among developers and technical teams before any enterprise contract. Our explainer on product-led growth covers when that motion fits and when it stalls.

Developers are also sceptical readers. Stack Overflow's 2025 survey of over 49,000 developers found 84% used or planned to use AI tools, but 46% did not trust the accuracy of their output, and technical documentation was the top learning resource at 68%. Docs that work on the first try are not a nicety. They are the sales process.

Marketplaces of the platforms you plug into

Most AI products live inside something else. A help desk, a CRM, a document store, a chat tool, a cloud provider, a model provider's app directory. Each has a marketplace, and the marketplace is a channel with trust already built in.

The cloud marketplaces matter most for enterprise deals because they double as procurement routes. AWS Marketplace charges SaaS sellers 3% on public offers and on private offers under $1 million in total contract value, falling to 2% from $1 million and 1.5% from $10 million and on all renewals. On Microsoft's marketplace, when a customer buys an "Azure benefit eligible" offer, 100% of the pre-tax amount counts toward their Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment. A buyer with unspent committed cloud budget may find it easier to buy you there than through a new vendor contract. Our pieces on marketplace listings for B2B sellers and co-selling with platforms cover private offers and partner programmes in detail.

Model-provider directories are newer and stricter than most founders expect. OpenAI's submission guidelines for apps in ChatGPT require a clear purpose and reliable function, a published privacy policy, collection of "only the minimum data required", and a fully featured demo account for review. They state that "trial or demo plugins will not be accepted" and reject apps that serve advertisements or use misleading tool descriptions to steer the model toward them.

The listing is a sales page. Treat it like one. Clear job, screenshots of the workflow, a demo video under two minutes, pricing in the open, reviews from real users.

Integration depth decides ranking and conversion. A shallow "connects to" integration gets listed. A deep one, that reads and writes the objects the buyer cares about, gets recommended by the platform's own team.

Platform typeWhat the listing must prove
Help desk or supportDraft quality or deflection, with a before and after
CRMData written back cleanly, no duplicate records
Cloud marketplacePrivate offer ready, commitment-eligible where possible, security pack attached
Model-provider directoryClear use case, minimal data collection, works on first run in review
Developer platformInstall in minutes, docs that match the current version

Answer-engine presence

Buyers now ask assistants before they search. "What tools help a finance team reconcile invoices?" If the assistant does not describe your product correctly, you are not in the consideration set.

The evidence is building. Gartner's survey of 645 B2B buyers, published in May 2026, found 45% had used generative AI during a purchase, mainly to research vendors and products, and 69% preferred to check AI-generated insights with a sales rep. Pew Research Center's tracking of 900 US adults found Google users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, against 15% without one, and clicked a link inside the summary on 1%. Pew's data is consumer search, not B2B, but the direction is clear: the summary is increasingly the whole answer.

Answer engines read what is public, plain and consistent. So put a one-paragraph product description on your site. What it does, who it is for, what it connects to. Repeat it, word for word, on marketplaces, directories and docs. Keep your pricing page readable as plain text. Publish comparison pages that are fair, because assistants quote them and buyers check. Our piece on how LLMs choose sources covers the mechanics.

Then test it. Ask several assistants what your product does and who it is for. Fix the gaps at the source. A press release does not fix a wrong answer. A clearer docs page does.

A press release does not fix a wrong answer. A clearer docs page does.

Content that demonstrates

AI buyers have seen enough claims pages. Show the product running on realistic data, end to end, with the mistakes left in. A twelve-minute recording of a real workflow converts better than a polished sixty-second montage, in our experience, because it answers the questions a sceptical buyer would otherwise ask the rep.

Publish the eval. If you claim accuracy, show the test set description, the method and the result, with a date. Those pages get cited by assistants and shared by engineers. They also feed the claims register from Part 11. Our explainer on AI evals covers what a readable eval contains.

Write for the person doing the job, not the person reading the deck.

Power users as distribution

Every AI product has a handful of users who build on it. Templates, prompts, workflows, integrations. They are your best channel, and they are cheap to serve.

Give them a place (Part 5), credit by name, early access and a way to publish what they built. A gallery of user-built workflows is both proof and a search surface. It also shows answer engines what the product is for, in the users' own words.

Paid last

Paid works when you know your activation rate and payback period (Part 9). Until then, paid in an AI category buys expensive clicks from people comparing twelve tabs. Put the budget into integration depth, the security pack and one good demonstration first.

CheckDone when
Lead motionOne chosen and written down, with the other two as support
MarketplacesListed on every platform you integrate with, with a demo video and a private offer route
Product paragraphIdentical across site, docs and listings
Answer enginesThree assistants asked what the product does; gaps fixed at the source
DemonstrationOne end-to-end recording and one published eval
Power usersGallery live, with credit by name

lowob takeaways

  • Choose one lead motion. Developer-led, sales-led or partner-led, with the others in support.
  • Treat marketplaces as procurement, not just discovery. Private offers and commitment eligibility move enterprise deals.
  • Write one plain product paragraph. Repeat it word for word across site, docs, marketplaces and directories, then test what assistants say.
  • Turn on paid last. Only once you know your activation rate and payback period.

Common questions

How do I get ChatGPT or other AI assistants to describe my product correctly?

Answer engines read what is public, plain and consistent. Put a one-paragraph product description on your site, repeat it word for word on marketplaces, directories and docs, keep pricing readable as plain text, then ask several assistants and fix gaps at the source.

Should an AI startup list on AWS or Azure Marketplace?

Yes, if enterprise buyers are the target. AWS charges SaaS sellers 3% on public offers and on private offers under $1 million, and eligible Azure Marketplace purchases count fully toward a customer's Azure consumption commitment, which can shorten procurement.

Should an early AI startup run developer-led, sales-led and partner-led at once?

No. Each needs a different company. Pick one to lead and let the others support; trying all three with one small team is how a seed-stage company spends a year reaching nobody.

When should an AI company start paid advertising?

Last, once you know your activation rate and payback period. Until then, paid in an AI category buys expensive clicks from people comparing twelve tabs.
